newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand, IMF complete work on policy package.
newsitem.headline: Thailand, IMF complete work on policy package.

text.p: Thailand and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday they had hammered out an policy package to accompany a $16 billion international loan to rescue the country's floundering economy.
An IMF official stressed that the credit package, which will be immediately ready for disbursements after IMF approval, could not be used to bail out Thailand's finance sector.

"The package should be an adequate response to the severe economic and financial difficulties with which the Thai economy presently faces," Hubert Neiss, head of the IMF team to Bangkok, told a news conference.
The agreed policy package must be reviewed by IMF management before being submitted to the IMF executive board for approval.
Neiss said the package should be submitted to the IMF executive board by the middle of next week and disbursements could begin immediately after approval was given.
A finance ministry source had said earlier that the IMF board is likely to approve the package by August 21.

Thailand is reeling from an economic crisis triggered by collapse in the financial and property sectors, leaving the currency battered and leading to the suspension of two thirds of the country's financial firms.
The IMF programme, details of which were not made available, must be used for specific ends, Neiss said.

"The fund provided by the IMF will be at disposal of the central bank of Thailand to replenish reserves...If the balance of payments is not covered by the long-term capital, this money can be used as and when necessary. The fund will absolutely not be used to clean up the finance sector," he said.

Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said he hope to use the fund as standby credit to control the situation but declined to speculate on the macro-economic picture at the end of the year after the policy package is implemented.
He said he did not expect 1997 inflation to surge to double digits after Thailand adopted tough austerity measures agreed in the IMF-sponsored package.
The government has announced it would raise its value added tax to 10 percent from seven percent from Aug 16 as part of its compliance with conditions in the IMF package.

The Thai consumers price index rose about 4.5 percent year-on-year during the first seven months of this year. Analysts expected inflation to rise to at least eight percent in the second half of the year.
